issues.legal_issue: Agrarian legislation acquiring estates and extinguishing intermediary rights is protected from challenges based on specified fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged laws acquired rights in inam estates and other covered lands, abolished intermediary holders, and established a direct relationship between the government and the occupants.
The laws formed part of an agrarian reform programme.
issues.conclusion: The laws could not be challenged as violating Articles 14, 19 or 31 because Article 31A protected legislation of this kind.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for the acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in an estate, or the extinguishment or modification of such rights, from invalidation under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The definition of estate in Article 31A(2) includes the relevant categories of land. The Court followed B. Shankara Rao Badami v. State of Mysore, [1969] 3 S.C.R. 1.

rule.if: agrarian_acquisition_proceeding and (state_acquires_estate_rights or state_extinguishes_intermediary_rights) and agrarian_reform_purpose

predicates.agrarian_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to legislation acquiring land or rights in land as part of an agrarian reform.
predicates.state_acquires_estate_rights: The legislation provides for the State to acquire an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.state_extinguishes_intermediary_rights: The legislation provides for the extinguishment or modification of intermediary rights in land.
predicates.agrarian_reform_purpose: The legislation forms part of a programme of agrarian reform.

issues.definition: When an agrarian acquisition proceeding concerns legislation that acquires estate rights or extinguishes intermediary rights for agrarian reform, the fundamental-rights challenge is barred.

issues.legal_issue: Land may remain an estate covered by the constitutional protection even if it ceased to be an inam, and an erroneous description of intermediaries does not invalidate legislation traceable to legislative power.
material_facts: Full assessment had been imposed on some lands under an earlier law, and the appellants argued that those lands had thereby ceased to be inams.
The Court held that such lands could still fall within the constitutional definition of an estate.
The legislation sought to abolish intermediaries, and any inaccurate description of some intermediaries did not defeat the legislation if it was supported by valid legislative power.
issues.conclusion: It was unnecessary to decide whether the lands had ceased to be inams: they remained estates within Article 31A if they fell within its defined categories. A mistaken description of intermediaries did not invalidate the legislation if it could be traced to valid legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a) defines estate to include categories of land beyond inams, including land held under ryotwari settlement and land held or let for agriculture or ancillary purposes. Legislation supported by valid legislative power is not invalid merely because the legislature wrongly described intermediaries it sought to remove.

predicates.agrarian_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to legislation acquiring land or rights in land as part of an agrarian reform.
predicates.land_falls_within_estate_definition: The land falls within a constitutionally defined category of estate, whether or not it remains classified as an inam.
predicates.legislation_has_valid_power: The legislation can be traced to a valid grant of legislative power.

issues.definition: If land falls within the estate definition and the legislation has valid legislative power, the protection applies despite a changed inam status or an inaccurate description of intermediaries.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of compensation for some properties within an acquired estate does not establish a violation of the compensation requirement where compensation is provided for the estate as a whole.
material_facts: The appellants contended that some properties included in an inam received no compensation.
The applicable law provided for compensation to be determined for each inam as a whole, and that provision was not challenged.
The Court proceeded on the assumption that some properties received no separate compensation.
issues.conclusion: The contention did not establish a violation of Article 31(2), because compensation was provided for the inam as a whole and Article 31A barred the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects qualifying estate acquisitions from a challenge under Article 31(2). The law provided for compensation to be determined for the inam as a whole rather than separately for each interest.

predicates.estate_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to the acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.compensation_provided_for_estate_as_a_wh: The acquisition scheme provides compensation determined for the estate as a whole.
predicates.no_separate_compensation_for_some_proper: Some property or interests within the estate receive no separate compensation.

issues.definition: When compensation is provided for the estate as a whole, the absence of separate compensation for some included property does not make the compensation challenge succeed.

issues.legal_issue: A court must presume, absent material to the contrary, that presidential assent was given after due consideration of the legislation's implications.
material_facts: The appellants asserted that the President had not been made aware of the implications of the bills when giving assent.
The record contained no material showing that the President or advisers were unaware of those implications.
issues.conclusion: The Court proceeded on the basis that the President had duly considered the implications before giving assent.
issues.legal_principle: In the absence of material to the contrary, the Court presumes that the President gave assent after duly considering the implications of the provisions. The assent was required by the first proviso to Article 31A.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: The case concerns a constitutional challenge to legislation requiring presidential assent.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President has given assent to the legislation.
predicates.no_evidence_of_lack_of_consideration: The record contains no material showing that the President or advisers failed to consider the legislation's implications.

issues.definition: If presidential assent was given and the record contains no evidence of lack of consideration, due consideration is presumed.

issues.legal_issue: A State legislature may legislate to reduce tenants' liability for arrears of rent or, alternatively, debts owed by agriculturists.
material_facts: The challenged laws reduced tenants' liability to pay arrears of rent, whether or not the arrears had been decreed.
The arrears could be treated either as rent arrears or as debts due from agriculturists.
issues.conclusion: The State legislature was competent to enact the provisions under either characterization of the arrears.
issues.legal_principle: Under Entry 18 of List II of the Seventh Schedule, the State legislature may legislate concerning rent. Under Entry 30 of List II, it may legislate concerning debts due from agriculturists.

predicates.tenant_liability_legislation: The case concerns legislation altering tenants' liability to pay arrears.
predicates.arrears_are_rent_or_agriculturist_debts: The arrears are either rent arrears or debts owed by agriculturists.

issues.definition: Legislation altering tenants' arrears liability is within State legislative competence when the arrears are rent or debts owed by agriculturists.

issues.legal_issue: Paying religious or charitable institutions compensation periodically rather than in a lump sum does not invalidate the acquisition.
material_facts: The acquired inams included property belonging to religious and charitable institutions.
The laws provided for a portion of compensation to be paid each year as tasdik rather than paying compensation in a lump sum.
The Court regarded this as a method of payment adopted in the institutions' interest.
issues.conclusion: The annual payment method did not violate Article 31(2) and was in any event protected by Article 31A.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) did not prohibit the method of paying compensation in annual portions in these circumstances. In any event, Article 31A protected the acquisition.

predicates.estate_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to the acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.institution_property_acquired: The acquired property belongs to a religious or charitable institution.
predicates.compensation_paid_in_periodic_portions: The acquisition scheme pays compensation in portions over time rather than as a lump sum.

issues.definition: When institutional property is acquired and compensation is paid in periodic portions, that payment method does not invalidate the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional right of a religious denomination to own, acquire and administer property does not prevent the State from acquiring that property.
material_facts: The appellants contended that acquisition of property belonging to religious denominations infringed their rights to own, acquire and administer property.
The Court held that acquisition caused the denominations to cease owning the property, after which their right to administer that property no longer applied.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional right to own, acquire and administer property did not take away the State's power to acquire property belonging to religious denominations.
issues.legal_principle: Article 26(c) and (d) protects a religious denomination's right to own and acquire property and to administer its property in accordance with law; it does not bar State acquisition of that property.

predicates.property_acquisition_challenge: The case concerns a challenge to the State's acquisition of property.
predicates.religious_denominational_property: The acquired property belongs to a religious denomination.

issues.definition: When the State acquires property belonging to a religious denomination, the denomination's property rights do not bar that acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A claim under the protection for personally cultivated land cannot be determined without evidence about personal cultivation and the applicable ceiling.
material_facts: An appellant argued that the acquisition contravened the second proviso to Article 31A because it affected personally cultivated property.
The record did not establish that any appellant's personally cultivated property had been acquired or what the applicable ceiling was.
issues.conclusion: The Court could not determine the claim on the available material, while observing that an acquisition would be invalid to the extent that the proviso was breached.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 31A protects qualifying land under personal cultivation, subject to the applicable ceiling. The Court required material showing both the relevant cultivation and the ceiling before examining the claim.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_proceeding and personal_cultivation_proviso_claim and (no_evidence_of_personal_cultivation_or_acquisition or no_evidence_of_applicable_ceiling)

predicates.estate_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to the acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.personal_cultivation_proviso_claim: A party claims that the acquisition affects land protected because it is under personal cultivation.
predicates.no_evidence_of_personal_cultivation_or_a: The record does not show that qualifying personally cultivated land was acquired.
predicates.no_evidence_of_applicable_ceiling: The record does not establish the applicable ceiling for the protected land.

issues.definition: A personal-cultivation protection claim cannot be decided on the record when evidence of the acquisition or the applicable ceiling is missing.

issues.legal_issue: Whether particular land falls within an inam-aboli­tion law's coverage should be determined through the statutory tribunal when that inquiry requires examination of the grant and other relevant materials.
material_facts: The appellants contended that the laws did not acquire or cover certain lands.
Determining the character and extent of the grants required examination of the grant terms and relevant materials.
A statutory tribunal was empowered to determine whether land fell within the relevant inam categories, and parties had applied to it in many cases.
issues.conclusion: The Court agreed that the coverage issue could be more appropriately determined by the tribunal and that dismissal of the writ proceedings did not prevent the inamdars from raising it there.
issues.legal_principle: The legislation provided a tribunal procedure for deciding whether land was within specified inam categories. The Court accepted that questions dependent on the terms and extent of grants were more appropriately determined through that procedure.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_coverage: The case is a writ challenge asserting that particular land is outside the coverage of an acquisition law.
predicates.coverage_depends_on_grant_evidence: Determining coverage requires examining the terms or extent of a grant and related evidence.
predicates.statutory_tribunal_can_determine_coverag: A statutory tribunal is empowered to determine whether the land falls within the law's covered categories.

issues.definition: When a writ coverage challenge depends on grant evidence and a statutory tribunal can decide coverage, the issue is left for that tribunal.
